description: How Gupta interweaves Rani's London survival story with Abdul Karim's rise at Queen Victoria's court.
content_html:
A Play of Two Worlds

Tanika Gupta’s The Empress spans two contrasting worlds that would never ordinarily appear on the same stage: the dockside poverty of Tilbury and the gilded interiors of Windsor Castle. The play opens in 1887, the year of Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, and follows its threads across roughly a decade and a half of the late Victorian era. Its two-act structure holds two parallel storylines in tension throughout, intercutting between them so that the audience builds understanding of both simultaneously.

Rani’s Storyline: Survival in the Imperial Metropolis

The play’s invented protagonist, Rani, is a young Indian ayah who arrives at Tilbury Docks as part of a British household’s return from India. At the play’s opening, in the scene at the docks, the English family pays Rani off and leaves her without passage home. From this moment of abandonment she must navigate a London that is simultaneously the capital of the Empire she has served and a city largely hostile to her presence.

Her journey takes her into the East End, where she discovers the Lascar sailors’ community — Indian and Yemeni seafarers who have long inhabited the port districts of London — and eventually to the Ayahs’ Home, a refuge in Hackney for stranded women in her position. Gupta uses Rani’s movement through these spaces to draw a social map of the hidden Indian presence in Victorian London: domestic servants, sailors and the first tentative signs of a South Asian political community.

Key Fact

Rani’s storyline begins at Tilbury Docks when the family she worked for pays her off without a return passage. She discovers the Lascar sailors’ community in the East End and the Ayahs’ Home in Hackney — both real Victorian institutions that Gupta draws on for historical authenticity.

Abdul Karim’s Storyline: Ascent at Court

Running in parallel is the story of Abdul Karim, a historical figure who arrived at Windsor Castle in 1887 as a servant for the Golden Jubilee celebrations and rose to become Queen Victoria’s Indian secretary — her munshi. In Gupta’s dramatisation, Victoria and Abdul develop a relationship of genuine personal warmth: she learns Hindustani from him, elevates his status and protects him against the fierce hostility of the court. Lord Salisbury, the Prince of Wales and the royal household circle perceive Abdul as an inappropriate favourite and move against him repeatedly throughout the play.

The court scenes are played in sharp contrast to the East End scenes: formal, spatially rigid, visually opulent. A director might choose a proscenium arch configuration for the Windsor scenes to reinforce their theatricality and hierarchy — the court literally arranges itself for display — while the Lascar lodgings and Ayahs’ Home might be played on a thrust stage area or in a more intimate configuration to reflect communal solidarity rather than spectacle.

The Intercut Structure and Its Effect

Gupta does not tell Rani’s story to completion and then tell Abdul’s. Instead she intercuts between them scene by scene, building a pattern of parallel storylines. This structural choice carries dramaturgical weight. Every time the audience moves from a Windsor Castle scene of court conspiracy to a scene of Rani sleeping in the Ayahs’ Home, the contrast asks a question: what does the Empire mean for someone at the very top of its hierarchy, and what does it mean for someone abandoned at its edges?

The intercut structure is itself a theatrical statement. A director staging this rhythm of cuts must think carefully about transitions: how quickly do scenes change? Does music bridge the cuts? Is the set design flexible enough to shift between Windsor’s formality and the East End’s working-world warmth without a clumsy scene change? In the original RSC 2013 premiere directed by Emma Rice, ensemble multi-roling and fluid staging kept transitions fast, so that the juxtaposition landed with impact rather than interruption.

Rani is Gupta’s invented protagonist, but she is grounded in real documented history. The Ayahs’ Home in Hackney and the Lascar communities of the East End are both historically attested. Gupta has compressed and dramatised: the Ayahs’ Home opened slightly later than 1887 in reality. Examiners reward students who recognise this as dramatic history — a playwright shaping fact for theatrical impact — rather than treating the play as a documentary record. Abdul Karim and Queen Victoria are historical; Rani and her immediate world are imaginatively reconstructed from evidence of real people in similar circumstances.

The Convergence and the Ending

The two storylines draw together near the play’s close. The moment of convergence — when Rani and figures from Abdul’s world briefly occupy the same space — offers the play’s most direct statement of solidarity. Structurally, this meeting is the fulfilment of the parallel design: two streams of late-Victorian Indian experience in Britain, briefly joined. The closing tableau asks the audience to hold in mind what has survived and what has been lost: Abdul’s papers were burned after Victoria’s death; the Ayahs’ Home closed; the Lascar community was gradually displaced.

Key Fact

The parallel, intercut structure is a deliberate dramaturgical choice: placing Rani’s world and Abdul’s world in constant dialogue means the audience cannot look at Imperial wealth without simultaneously holding in mind its human cost at street level.

When a director works on the cuts between storylines in The Empress, a useful checklist includes: (1) Lighting states — a lighting state using warm amber and gold for Windsor against a cooler, more natural white wash for the East End scenes will encode the contrast in the audience’s visual memory. (2) Underscore — Hindi or Hindustani song cues between scenes can act as bridges that carry the emotional thread of the Indian characters even into the English spaces. (3) Blocking — the physical geography of Windsor scenes (courtiers fanning out upstage in hierarchical lines) versus the East End scenes (characters gathered centre stage in an impromptu circle) communicates social structure through space alone.
exam_tip_html: For extended-response questions about structure and staging, the most common error is describing the two storylines separately rather than explaining why Gupta intercuts them and what effect that creates on an audience. Always make the juxtaposition explicit: say what the audience is made to feel or think when the Windsor scene is followed immediately by the East End scene. For a 20-mark extended staging response, you must address both performer choices and design discipline choices — do not spend all your time on lighting and forget to specify vocal or physical choices for a named character in a named moment of the structural intercut.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Empress uses a two-act structure with parallel intercut storylines: Rani’s survival story in the East End and Abdul Karim’s rise at Windsor Castle, both set in the 1887–1901 period.
  • Gupta’s structural choice to intercut rather than separate the storylines means the audience constantly holds both worlds in mind, creating dramatic irony and political contrast.
  • Directors must make active choices about how to stage transitions — through lighting state changes, underscored music and blocking patterns — to keep the intercutting fluid and the juxtaposition impactful.

practice_questions.text: Name the historical event that took place in 1887 and provides the opening context of The Empress.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee (accept: the Jubilee celebrations / the 50th anniversary of Victoria's reign).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'parallel storylines' in a play?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that two or more separate narrative threads run alongside each other; 1 mark for explaining that these threads are intercut or juxtaposed so that each illuminates the other (accept equivalent explanation).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could use contrasting lighting states when the play moves between the Windsor Castle scenes and the East End scenes in The Empress. Refer to specific lighting choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific Windsor lighting choice (1) such as a warm amber or gold wash to signal wealth and formality; identification of a contrasting East End lighting choice (1) such as a cooler white or pale blue wash to suggest poverty and natural London light; explanation of the effect on the audience of the contrast (1) e.g. the shift encodes social hierarchy visually so the audience is reminded of inequality with every transition; link to the play's structural meaning (1) e.g. the lighting state contrast reinforces Gupta's dramaturgical juxtaposition of the two worlds of the British Empire.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the structure of The Empress — specifically the intercut parallel storylines — creates dramatic tension for the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the intercut structure (1); explanation of the technique's effect, e.g. that cutting between Rani's vulnerability and the court's opulence creates irony (1); analysis of how the structure builds towards the convergence near the play's end (1); reference to a specific named moment in one of the two storylines (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Gupta's intentions in choosing to open The Empress with the scene at Tilbury Docks in which Rani is paid off and abandoned. What does Gupta want the audience to think and feel at this moment?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Detailed analysis of Gupta's multiple intentions — to establish Rani's vulnerability as the audience's entry point into the play; to make the systemic nature of the ayahs' exploitation concrete and immediate rather than abstract; to root the play's political argument in a personal, emotionally engaging story. Candidate links these intentions to specific dramatic methods (the choice of a public dockside setting, the power imbalance in staging terms, the contrast between Rani's isolation and the bustle of the docks) and explains the intended audience effect at each. Substantiated judgement about which intention is primary.

Secure (7–9): Two of the above intentions clearly articulated with some reference to dramatic methods; the effect on the audience is identified though not always fully developed.

Developing (4–6): One intention identified; limited reference to dramatic method; effect on audience implied rather than explained.

Emerging (1–3): Describes what happens at the docks rather than analysing why Gupta chose to begin there and what she wants the audience to understand.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the moment in The Empress when the two storylines converge near the play's end and characters from Rani's world and Abdul's world briefly share the stage. How would you stage this moment to communicate the play's themes of solidarity and survival to the audience? Refer to set design, lighting, sound and at least one performer's vocal or physical choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17–20): Specific, justified choices across all four design disciplines and at least one named performer's vocal and physical choices, all anchored to this named convergence moment. Set design choice (e.g. the divide between the Windsor staging area and the East End area dissolving as characters cross the stage threshold), lighting choice (e.g. a slow cross-fade from two separate lighting states into a unified warm gold wash as the characters meet), sound choice (e.g. a Hindi underscore that swells as they converge, then holds under the final dialogue), costume contrast still legible onstage (Rani's worn sari fabric against Abdul's court livery). Performer choice: specific vocal quality and physical positioning (proxemics) for Rani in this moment. Choices are justified with reference to what the audience is meant to feel. Substantiated directorial judgement.

Secure (11–16): Most of the design areas covered with some concrete choices; at least one named performer choice; effect on audience identified for most choices.

Developing (6–10): Some relevant staging ideas but generic (e.g. 'warm lighting', 'Indian music'); little justification of how each choice creates meaning; performer choices vague.

Emerging (1–5): Basic listing of staging ideas with minimal explanation; no named performer choices; descriptive rather than analytical.

knowledge_checks.q: In which year is the opening of The Empress set?
What is the term for a frozen stage picture held by performers at the end of a scene?
Rani is abandoned at _____ Docks at the start of The Empress.
A _____ storyline structure means two narrative threads are intercut within the same play.
Match each term to its meaning:
right: An Indian nanny or nursemaid employed by colonial families
An Indian secretary or teacher; Victoria's title for Abdul Karim
A frozen stage picture held by performers at the end of a scene

flashcard_questions.q: Who is Rani in The Empress?
flashcard_questions.a: Gupta's invented protagonist, a young Indian ayah abandoned in London in 1887.
An Indian woman employed as a children's nanny by colonial families, often stranded in Britain.
An Indian teacher or secretary; the title Queen Victoria used for Abdul Karim.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'parallel storylines' mean in drama?
flashcard_questions.a: Two or more separate narrative threads running side by side, intercut within the same play.
A frozen stage picture held by performers, creating a final image for the audience.
The complete combination of on-stage lanterns, colours, intensities and directions at one moment.
Continuous music or sound running beneath scenes to maintain atmosphere or signal a change of world.
The planned arrangement of performers' positions on stage, decided by the director.

flashcard_questions.q: The Empress premiered at which theatre in which year?
Who directed the original 2013 RSC premiere of The Empress?
Why does Gupta intercut the two storylines rather than tell them separately?
flashcard_questions.a: To place Imperial wealth and street-level poverty in constant dramatic contrast for the audience.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a proscenium arch stage?
flashcard_questions.a: A stage where the audience sits on one side, facing a framed opening, typical of Victorian theatres.

glossary_terms.definition: An Indian woman employed as a children's nanny or nursemaid by British colonial families, often left stranded when the family returned to Britain without arranging her return passage.
An Indian teacher or secretary; the title Queen Victoria used for Abdul Karim, who taught her Hindustani.
Two or more separate narrative threads in a play, intercut scene by scene so that each storyline illuminates the other.
A frozen stage picture held by performers at the end of a scene or play, creating a final visual image.
The complete combination of lanterns, colours, intensities and directions active on stage at any given moment in a production.
Continuous music or sound running beneath scenes to maintain atmosphere or signal a shift between worlds.
The planned arrangement of performers on stage, including their positions, movements and spatial relationships, decided by the director.
A stage configuration in which the audience sits on one side, facing a framed stage opening, common in Victorian and Edwardian theatres.
A stage that extends into the audience area on three sides, surrounding the action on three edges of the playing space.
